gdp.note: FAO estimates 2025 ON GDP at 1.3%. Q4 2025 little changed after +0.5% Q3.

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Ontario's unemployment rate held at 7.6% in the March Labour Force Survey1, unchanged from February, as Q4 2025 employment gains of +58,900 (+0.7%) absorbed into a stable base after two preceding weak quarters. The Financial Accountability Office estimates 2025 Ontario real GDP at 1.3%, down from 1.6% in 2024, with the Q4 2025 economy little changed after a +0.5% Q3 rebound.2 The employment rate held flat at 59.7% while the participation rate carried at 64.6%, 0.2 percentage points above the prior observation.1 Ontario's year-over-year CPI reading of -1.8% is the lowest provincial print in Canada and widened 0.7 percentage points below the prior reading of -1.1%, standing 3.6 percentage points below the national +1.8% figure.3

Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy tabled the Ontario Budget 2026 on March 26, raising the ten-year capital plan to $210 billion (up $9 billion from the prior framework), with $37 billion allocated for 2026-27 and approximately $64 billion over ten years for health infrastructure including roughly 50 hospital projects and 3,000 new beds.4 Infrastructure spending for 2025-28 increased $13.6 billion from the Fall Economic Statement. The budget confirmed $31 billion over ten years for highway investment, with construction underway on Highway 413 (52 km, supporting 6,000 jobs per year), the Bradford Bypass, and Highway 7 expansion between Kitchener and Guelph.5 The Ring of Fire all-season road construction is now targeted for June 2026, with roads opening November 2030 — five years ahead of the prior timeline.6

Ontario's goods exports to the United States fell 4.0% in 2025, while exports to the rest of the world rose 17.0%, reflecting trade diversification as the effective tariff rate on Ontario exports to the U.S. exceeds 6%.2 Housing starts rose 2.3% to 67,274 units (SAAR) in March, up from 65,757 the prior month.7 Building permits stood at $2,690.8 million in the latest StatCan print.8 The project database tracks the Ontario Line ($27.4B, Under Construction), GO Expansion ($26.1B, Under Construction), the Deep Geological Repository ($26.0B, Proposed), and the Bruce Nuclear Refurbishment ($13.0B, Under Construction) as the province's largest active capital files.9

gdp.note: 2026 GDP forecast 1.1%. Q4 2025 real GDP -0.1% q/q (ISQ).

unemployment.note: Drop reflects fewer seekers, not net hiring.

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Quebec's unemployment rate fell 0.5 percentage points to 5.4% in March1, though the decline reflects fewer active job seekers rather than net hiring — employment was little changed after a -57,000 loss in February. The participation rate edged down 0.1 percentage points to 64.4%, while the employment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 60.9%.1 Quebec City CMA posted unemployment of 2.6%, the lowest metropolitan reading in Canada.1 The Institut de la statistique du Québec recorded Q4 2025 real GDP at -0.1% quarter-over-quarter, with the 2026 GDP forecast at 1.1%.2

The Quebec Budget 2026-2027, tabled during week one of this edition window, committed $167 billion in the ten-year Quebec Infrastructure Plan (QIP) over 2026-2036, of which 71% ($105.8 billion) is designated for asset maintenance.3 The QIP allocates $35.7 billion for roads, $24.7 billion for health, $23.5 billion for education, $12.8 billion for transit, and $8.9 billion for IT infrastructure.3 An additional $1.7 billion is earmarked for economic transformation initiatives. The province also announced an $8 billion Transport Plan for 2026-2028 covering road, maritime, rail, and airport infrastructure, with 77% directed toward asset maintenance.4

Manufacturing GDP in U.S.-trade-reliant industries contracted approximately 4% between December 2024 and November 20255, as the effective tariff rate on Quebec exports to the United States exceeds 6%. CPI ran at +0.6% year-over-year in February, down 0.1 percentage points from the prior reading.6 Housing starts rose 2.8% to 53,461 units (SAAR).7 The project database tracks the Parc éolien Chamouchouane wind farm ($9.0B, Proposed), the Montreal Metro Blue Line Extension ($4.9B, Under Construction, completion 2031), the TES Canada Hydrogen facility in Shawinigan ($4.0B, Under Review), and the Quebec City Tramway ($3.8B, Under Construction, completion 2033).8 The Timiskaming Dam-Bridge environmental assessment decision deadline was extended on March 9.9

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Alberta's unemployment rate rose 0.2 percentage points to 6.5% in March1, edging up despite approximately 85,000 jobs added over the prior year. ATB Financial upgraded the 2026 GDP forecast to 2.7% (from 2.1%) based on a WTI assumption of US$75/bbl, while the provincial budget baseline uses 1.8%.2 The participation rate slipped 0.3 percentage points to 68.7%, and the employment rate edged down 0.1 percentage points to 64.4%.1 ATB forecasts job creation of 3.1% for 2026.2

The Alberta Budget 2026, tabled in week one of this edition window, projects a $9.4 billion deficit as oilsands royalties dropped $7.5 billion from 2024-25 levels.3 Non-renewable resource cash revenue stands at $13.2 billion, down $8.8 billion from the prior fiscal year.3 The budget includes a $28.3 billion provincial capital plan. The Trans Mountain Expansion (TMX) pipeline scaled crude oil shipments to Asia to over $9 billion in 2025, supporting diversification of Alberta's export markets away from the United States.4 Geopolitical disruptions, including tensions around Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, have been cited in oil price revision analyses.4

Alberta CPI accelerated to +4.8% year-over-year in February, up 1.4 percentage points from the prior print, the second-highest provincial reading after PEI.5 Housing starts slipped 0.9% to 48,438 units (SAAR).6 Building permits stood at $1,127.1 million.7 The Pathways Alliance carbon capture and storage project ($16.5B, Proposed) and AOSP Jackpine oil sands development ($12.0B, Approved) are the province's largest proposed and approved energy files, while Telus infrastructure investment ($19.0B, Under Construction, through 2027) represents the largest non-energy capital commitment.8

provinces.name: British Columbia

unemployment.note: Highest since Feb 2016 (ex-pandemic). Matches national rate.

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
British Columbia shed 19,000 jobs (-0.7%) in March following a -20,000 loss in February — two consecutive months of employment declines totalling 39,000 positions.1 Unemployment rose 0.6 percentage points to 6.7%, the highest reading since February 2016 outside of the pandemic period, and now matches the national rate.1 Job losses concentrated in retail and wholesale (approximately 10,000), finance and real estate, and professional and technical services. Manufacturing (+3,700) and construction (+2,800) recorded gains.1 The participation rate fell 0.4 percentage points to 64.4% and the employment rate declined 0.4 percentage points to 60.5%.2

The province's rental market continued to soften. Apartment asking rents fell 4.8% year-over-year in March, with purpose-built rents down 12.2% from the August 2023 peak.3 Housing starts edged down 0.4% to 41,331 units (SAAR).4 CPI ran at +1.3% year-over-year in February, up 0.3 percentage points from the prior reading but still below the national average.5 Building permits stood at $1,121.9 million.6

In week two of this edition window, British Columbia expanded employment services on April 16, announcing new training projects to address the labour market deterioration.7 LNG Canada Phase 1 ($47.9B, Under Construction) in Kitimat remains the province's largest active project, with the proposed Phase 2 ($25.0B) awaiting a final investment decision. The Site C hydroelectric dam ($16.0B, Under Construction) on the Peace River and the Kitimat Clean Oil Refinery ($22.0B, Under Review) round out the province's mega-project pipeline.8 Sub-trend GDP growth is expected through 2026.9

provinces.name: Saskatchewan

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Saskatchewan posted the lowest unemployment rate in the country at 5.0% in March, down 0.6 percentage points from February, as employment rose 5,800 (+0.9%) — the strongest provincial employment growth rate nationally.1 Full-time employment added 15,000 positions year-over-year.1 CPI swung to +1.0% year-over-year in February from -0.7% the prior month, a reversal of 1.7 percentage points.2 Housing starts rose 3.0% to 5,486 units (SAAR).3

BHP's Jansen Stage 1 potash mine ($7.5B, Under Construction) is on track to begin production in late 2026, with capacity of approximately 8.5 million tonnes per annum and 3,500 construction jobs and 900 permanent positions.4 Jansen Stage 2 ($6.4B, Under Construction) is proceeding in parallel. January mineral sales totalled $1.2 billion (+0.1% year-over-year), though potash sales fell 6.5%, uranium declined 16.3%, and salt dropped 57.3% in the same period.5

The Saskatchewan capital budget for 2026-27 totals $4.3 billion.6 The proposed Federated Co-operatives (FCL) hydrogenation-derived renewable diesel plant ($2.0B) and Bell AI Data Centre ($1.7B, RM of Sherwood) represent diversification plays beyond the province's traditional potash and uranium resource base.7 Building permits stood at $154.4 million.8

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Manitoba employment surged 11,000 (+1.5%) in March — the strongest gain nationally — rebounding from February declines.1 Unemployment edged down 0.1 percentage points to 5.6%.1 The participation rate carried at 66.3%, down 0.8 percentage points from the prior observation, while the employment rate stood at 62.5%.2 CPI rose 0.3 percentage points to +3.4% year-over-year in February, the third-highest provincial reading nationally.3

Canada and Manitoba signed a new assessment agreement on April 14 (week two of this edition window), implementing the "one project, one review" framework to streamline major project approvals.4 Manitoba Budget 2026 includes a record $3.8 billion capital investment, 40% more apprenticeship positions, and the Port of Churchill Plus program at $262.5 million over five years with a $10 million Catalyst Fund.5 Manitoba's exports to the United States fell 18% year-over-year, concentrated in energy, agricultural machinery, and pharmaceuticals — among the worst trade-exposure readings nationally.6

The NEWPCC wastewater treatment upgrade ($3.2B, Under Construction) in Winnipeg is the province's largest active infrastructure project. Portage Place redevelopment ($650M, Under Construction) is creating a healthcare centre of excellence in downtown Winnipeg. The Lake Manitoba and Lake St. Martin outlet channels ($495M, Approved) address flood mitigation.7 Housing starts fell 2.0% to 7,642 units (SAAR) and building permits stood at $231.5 million.89

provinces.name: Nova Scotia

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Nova Scotia's unemployment rate fell 0.5 percentage points to 6.6% in March, with employment rising 3,900 (+0.7%).1 Halifax CMA unemployment stood at 6.1%, up 0.2 percentage points.1 Halifax GDP grew 2.3% in 2025, with a forecast of 1.5% for 2026.2 The participation rate carried at 61.3% and the employment rate at 57.0%.3 CPI rose 0.2 percentage points to +1.7% year-over-year in February.4

The Nova Scotia Legislature concluded its session on April 9 (week two of this edition window), passing Budget 2026-27 and the Powering the Economy Act, which establishes a regulatory framework for offshore wind, geothermal, hydrogen, and carbon storage.5 Offshore wind bid requirements include a $250,000 refundable deposit, $750,000 non-refundable fee, and $7,000 per MW per year.5 Canada and Nova Scotia signed a new assessment agreement on March 27 implementing the "one project, one review" framework.6 The province allocated $300 million for 1,430 homes including 930 units at Shannon Park, and $873.8 million for 5,700 long-term care spaces by 2032.5

Housing starts totalled 7,146 units (SAAR) in March, down 1.5% from the prior month, following a 2025 provincial record of 9,760 units.7 The province introduced a First Time Homebuyers Pilot enabling 2% down payments via provincial credit unions.5 Bear Head Energy ($8.0B, Proposed) is the province's largest energy project, while the NS Capital Plan 2026-27 ($3.5B) includes health and housing commitments. CFB Halifax Upgrade ($1.2B) and 14 Wing Greenwood Hangar ($648M) reflect federal defence investment in the province.8 Building permits stood at $242.9 million.9

provinces.analysis:
New Brunswick's unemployment held steady at 7.0% in March, unchanged from February, with employment little changed over the period.1 The participation rate edged up 0.1 percentage points to 60.7% and the employment rate held at 56.5%.2 CPI accelerated 1.2 percentage points to +2.4% year-over-year in February.3 GDP forecast for 2026-27 averages 1.3%.4

NB Power filed two applications with the Energy and Utilities Board during week one, covering reliability improvements and revenue stabilization, as a governance review proceeded through March 31.5 The utility plans to add 1,400 MW of new wind capacity by 2035, a fivefold increase from the current 355 MW, with four Indigenous-partnered power purchase agreements signed.5 NB Power's generation mix is 44% renewable and 80% non-emitting. Immigration allocations rose to 4,250 nominations, up 1,500, with $54.3 million allocated over three years via Opportunities NB.6

Housing starts fell 6.9% to 6,011 units (SAAR) and building permits stood at $131.9 million.78 Eleven SREP-funded projects totalling $112 million are underway in the province.5 The Saint John Pulp Mill upgrade ($1.1B, Under Review) is the province's largest proposed manufacturing file. Route 2 Trans-Canada Highway twinning ($420M) and Port Saint John terminal modernization ($205M) are under construction.9 Premier Holt is scheduled to meet Prime Minister Carney on April 20-21 to discuss defence and energy priorities.6

provinces.name: Newfoundland and Labrador

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Newfoundland and Labrador's unemployment rate rose 0.3 percentage points to 9.5% in March — the highest provincial reading in Canada — despite ongoing offshore project ramp-ups.1 The offshore petroleum sector accounts for approximately 20% of provincial GDP and 55% of exports.2 The participation rate carried at 58.1%, up 0.5 percentage points from the prior observation, and the employment rate at 52.7%, up 0.4 percentage points.3 CPI rose 0.5 percentage points to +2.3% year-over-year in February.4

The Province reached a benefits agreement with Equinor and BP on the Bay du Nord deepwater oil project during week one — the first standalone offshore development since Hebron. The agreement covers 3 million fabrication hours, 31 million person-hours over 25 years, and up to $6.4 billion in Phase 1 revenue, including royalties, local benefits, and an equity option.5 West White Rose topsides and concrete gravity structure installation and drilling are underway, extending the White Rose field's production life.6 The Point Rousse Port received an IAAC early decision on February 18 confirming no further assessment is required.7

Offshore employment totalled 20,500 jobs (8.4% of the provincial workforce) in 2024, with wages ranging from $80,000 to over $150,000.2 Housing starts edged up 2.4% to 1,223 units (SAAR) and building permits stood at $74.1 million.89 The Grassy Point LNG facility ($10.0B, Proposed), Bay du Nord ($6.4B, Approved), and Kami mining project ($3.86B, Under Review) compose the province's deepest project pipeline, with tariff exposure below 1% given the offshore orientation of NL exports.2

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Prince Edward Island's CPI reached +7.3% year-over-year in February — the highest provincial reading in Canada, 5.5 percentage points above the national +1.8% figure — accelerating 1.9 percentage points from the prior +5.4%.1 At the same time, the province posted the fastest average weekly earnings growth nationally at 5.5% (through November 2025), with average weekly earnings reaching $1,126.63.2 Unemployment edged up 0.1 percentage points to 7.3% in March.3

Employment reached an all-time high of 95,500 in January 2026, up 1,500 year-over-year.2 The participation rate stood at 66.6% (+0.1pp) and the employment rate at 61.8% (+0.3pp).4 Canada and PEI signed an assessment agreement in March 2026 implementing the "one project, one review" framework for major project approvals.5

Housing starts fell 13.4% to 963 units (SAAR) and building permits stood at $24.1 million.67 The PEI capital budget for 2026-27 totals $486 million, part of a five-year $1.6 billion plan covering healthcare and education.2 The PEI Mental Health Campus ($131M, Under Construction) in Charlottetown, Affordable Housing development ($100M, 300+ units, Proposed), and Northumberland Strait Cable ($92M, Under Construction) are the province's tracked projects.8

provinces.name: Yukon

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Yukon's unemployment held at 3.9% in March, unchanged from February and the lowest territorial rate.1 The 2024 annual GDP contracted 3.3%.2 CPI, housing starts, and participation rate are not published at the territorial level. Mineral spending in the territory totalled $313 million in 2025, of which $241.7 million was exploration expenditure.3

The federal and territorial governments approved the Kudz Ze Kayah copper-lead-zinc mine on April 15 (week two of this edition window), despite opposition from the Kaska Nation.4 BMC Minerals plans to mine 2 million tonnes per year over 10 years, which would make it Canada's largest zinc producer. The territory tightened mining approval timelines and launched an online bonding calculator and live project tracking system during the two-week window.5 The Yukon-BC Grid Connect is in early planning stages, with the North Canol corridor tied to both the Macmillan Pass and Mactung mineral deposits.3

The Casino Mine ($3.62B, Proposed) — a copper-gold-molybdenum project — is the territory's largest proposed mining development. Whitehorse Power Centres ($520M, Proposed) and the Yukon Capital Plan ($385M) round out the active project pipeline. Federal Northern Defence spending ($40.0B, Proposed) would include Yukon-based components if advanced.6

provinces.name: Northwest Territories

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
The Northwest Territories recorded the largest unemployment increase nationally in March, surging 0.8 percentage points to 6.1% from 5.3% in February.1 The spike reflects the ongoing wind-down of the territory's diamond mining sector. The Diavik diamond mine completed final production after 23 years and 150 million carats, marking the closure of one of three mines that at peak employed over 1,500 NWT residents and generated approximately 20% of territorial GDP.2

The diamond industry has channelled over $30 billion into the Canadian economy over 25 years, of which $20 billion flowed through the NWT.2 Two diamond mines remain operational: Gahcho Kue (De Beers, producing until 2031) and Ekati (projected operations to 2040).2 The Tlicho Government, Yellowknives Dene First Nation, and GNWT signed a partnership agreement to support workers and communities through the structural transition.3 Territorial leaders are pivoting to critical minerals — a strategy requiring more but smaller mines than the diamond model.2

The 2024 annual GDP contracted 1.1%.4 CPI and housing starts are not published at the territorial level. The Mackenzie Valley Highway ($2.0B, Approved) and Taltson Hydro Expansion ($2.0B, Approved) are the territory's largest approved infrastructure projects. The Pine Point lead-zinc mine ($653M, Under Review) represents the critical minerals pivot in practice. Federal Arctic Defence spending ($35.0B, Proposed) would include NWT components.5

provinces.name: Nunavut

unemployment.note: March rate not enumerated for Nunavut.

wageGrowth.note: Provincial wage-growth series not published for this region; using national average earnings growth as a proxy.

provinces.analysis:
Nunavut's unemployment rate stands at approximately 13.8% (three-month average through January 2026) — the highest rate in Canada — reflecting structural barriers to employment in remote communities despite active mining operations.1 The March rate is not separately enumerated for Nunavut. The 2024 annual GDP grew 7.5%, the strongest rate among all provinces and territories.2 CPI and housing starts are not published at the territorial level.

The territory hosts three gold mines producing over 1.2 million ounces per year, alongside world-class iron ore deposits and a growing critical minerals pipeline.3 Baffinland concluded Inuit consultation on the Steensby Component during this edition window, with rail-and-port construction planned for 2026.3 The Baffinland Steensby Expansion ($3.0B, Approved) would create the territory's first railway. B2Gold's Goose Mine installed a CleanDesign hybrid energy system, reducing diesel consumption by approximately 4,000 litres per day.4

The Grays Bay Port and Road project proposes a 900-km road connecting the Arctic coast to southern infrastructure, part of a broader federal commitment of over $40 billion for northern infrastructure and critical minerals development.5 The 750 Homes Initiative ($480M, Under Construction) addresses acute housing need in the territory's communities. Back River Gold ($610M, Under Construction) and federal Northern Defence spending ($32.0B, Proposed) round out the project pipeline. Nunavut land-use plan negotiations continue amid increased mining interest.6
